candidates.source_name: Cyril of Alexandria / Commentary on the Gospel of John
candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk VII.4 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's response to Lazarus's sickness — 'This sickness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, that the Son of God might be glorified thereby' — Cyril reads with characteristic providential precision. 'Not unto death' does NOT deny the impending physical death of Lazarus (which occurs and is graphically described) but rather denies death's TERMINUS character: death will not be the final word, glory will. 'That the Son of God might be glorified' Cyril takes as showing Christ's deliberate ordering of the entire sequence — including the delay (vv. 6-7) — toward the eschatological self-revelation. The Tewahedo Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase preserves this providential reading in its prayers over the dying: every sickness is potentially the occasion for divine glory.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk VII.11 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's announcement — 'Our friend Lazarus sleepeth (kekoimētai)' — Cyril notes establishes the patristic-liturgical vocabulary for Christian death: the dead 'sleep' (koimēsis, Latin dormitio) rather than 'die' in the pagan-tragic sense. The verb implies awakening; sleep is not termination but pause. Cyril builds his entire doctrine of Christian death from this: the cemetery (koimētērion) is etymologically a 'sleeping-place' awaiting resurrection. The disciples' literal-minded misreading ('if he sleep, he shall do well') Christ corrects (v. 14: 'Lazarus is dead'), but Cyril preserves the original metaphor as theologically correct: Lazarus's death is a sleep precisely because of what Christ is about to do to it.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk VII.25 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'I am the resurrection, and the life' (egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē) — the fifth of Christ's 'I AM' sayings in John — Cyril reads as the climactic ontological self-disclosure of the Word in His resurrection-power. Christ does not say 'I cause' resurrection or 'I bring' resurrection but 'I AM' resurrection — He is Himself the active principle of bodily restoration from death. 'And the life' Cyril takes as the deeper ontological foundation: resurrection-of-the-dead presupposes life-as-such which Christ IS by nature. Against any reading that would make Christ a powerful intermediary, Cyril insists the verse predicates of Christ what is predicable only of God. This is the textual heart of Cyril's resurrection-Christology.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die' Cyril treats with careful eschatological precision: 'never die' (ou mē apothanē eis ton aiōna) does NOT deny the universal experience of bodily death (which Christians clearly continue to experience) but denies death's POWER as a permanent severance from God. The believer dies physically but is not dead spiritually; the body sleeps but the soul lives in Christ; the resurrection at the last day reunites and consummates. This realized-eschatology reading is paired with the future-eschatology of v. 24-25; Cyril holds both together as the proper Christian doctrine of death and resurrection — fully realized in part now, awaiting full consummation.

candidates.source_attribution: Cyril of Alexandria, Commentary on John, Bk VII.35 (NPNF S2 V14). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

The shortest verse in the Gospel — 'Jesus wept' (edakrysen ho Iēsous) — Cyril expounds at length as decisive for orthodox Christology against three errors at once. (1) Against the Apollinarian denial of Christ's true human soul (Christ wept with real human grief, possessing human affections). (2) Against the Docetist denial of true incarnation (the tears were real tears, not theatrical). (3) Against any Stoic reading of impassibility-applied-to-Christ (Christ's incarnate nature genuinely felt sorrow). Yet Cyril carefully preserves the divine nature's impassibility: the WEEPING is predicated of the one Person via the assumed humanity, not of the divine essence in itself. This is Miaphysite Christology applied to a single verse — load-bearing for Tewahedo dogmatic theology.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Said I not unto thee, that, if thou wouldest believe, thou shouldest see the glory of God' Cyril reads as the principle that faith is the epistemic condition for perceiving divine glory. Martha's prior hesitation ('by this time he stinketh') is gently rebuked; Christ reframes the situation: belief is not response to the miracle but PRECONDITION for properly perceiving it. The 'glory of God' Cyril takes here as denoting both the resurrection-miracle about to occur AND the eternal Glory of the Son which the miracle makes visible. The Tewahedo liturgical posture before consecration — the faithful stand in reverent silence, the deacon calls 'Let us attend' — embodies this Cyrilline principle: faith first, vision second.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

Christ's prayer of thanksgiving — 'Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me' — Cyril carefully defends against any subordinationist reading. The prayer is not informational request (as if the Son needed to ask the Father for power) but liturgical-pedagogical: spoken for the benefit of the bystanders to manifest the unbroken Trinitarian communion. 'Thou hast heard me' (in the perfect tense — ēkousas) Cyril reads as evidencing the eternal mutual-knowing of Father and Son: the Father has eternally 'heard' because the Son and Father share one divine knowledge. The prayer is the incarnate Word's pedagogical disclosure of what is always already eternally true.

Cyril of Alexandria Commentary on the Gospel of John (c. 428 AD)

'Lazarus, come forth' (Lazare, deuro exō) — Cyril notes the cosmic significance of the imperative addressed to a corpse. The verb 'come forth' presupposes a hearer capable of obeying; Christ speaks to Lazarus as already living, since His Word IS life-giving. The naming 'Lazarus' Cyril takes as theologically precise: Christ calls only this one out of the tomb (else, the patristic tradition observes, all the dead would have risen). This personal-specific calling prefigures the eschatological resurrection where each believer is called by name. The Tewahedo Easter Anaphora's prayer 'arise, my soul, from the dust' explicitly echoes this Lazarus pattern.
